query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their mechanical and thermoelastic behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The mechanical and thermoelastic behavior of refractory high-entropy alloys can be explained by the valence electron concentration (VEC) and the resulting elastically isotropic deformation behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloys with a single BCC solid solution microstructure
generation.intervention: Variation of the valence electron concentration (VEC) through alloy design
generation.mechanism: The VEC influences the bond lengths and atomic interactions in the unit cell, leading to unique elastic and plastic deformation behaviors
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved mechanical properties, such as yield strength and work-hardening exponent, and excellent phase stability at elevated temperatures
generation.baseline: Conventional BCC alloys with a narrow distribution of interatomic distances
generation.boundary: The validity of the theoretical calculation methods to design elastically isotropic and ductile BCC HEAs
generation.uncertainty: The experimental validation of the predicted unusual deformation behaviors and the lack of strong temperature-dependent elastic anisotropic deformation behavior

falsification_experiment.design: In situ neutron experiments and theoretical approaches to investigate the elastic and plastic deformation behavior of refractory HEAs
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental results do not show the predicted elastically isotropic behavior and improved mechanical properties, the hypothesis is falsified.

In contrast to conventional BCC alloys that have a narrow distribution of interatomic distances, HEAs have a wider variety of bond lengths and atomic interactions in the unit cell, which may play a role in the unique elastic and plastic deformation behaviors at RT and high temperatures.
Recently, Tian et al. () suggested alloy design strategies to develop elastically isotropic HEAs (TiZrNbMoVx systems) using state-of-the-art ab initio simulations. According to their calculations, the TiZrNbMoyVx [where (x, y) are (0, 0.9) and (0.5, 0.8)] refractory HEAs exhibit the elastically isotropic deformation behavior, which is strongly correlated to the value of the valence electron concentration (VEC) (). Furthermore, these previous investigations provide criteria to evaluate the brittle-ductile behaviors based on single-crystal elastic constants, predicting that a few BCC HEA systems can be ductile (). Moreover, we investigated the type of mobile dislocations using the neutron diffraction (ND) peak-broadening modeling and analysis using the Williamson-Hall plot method (), experimentally verified by the high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) technique. It is found that the dominant type of mobile dislocations during plastic deformation could be edge dislocations, which is different from conventional BCC metals. These new discoveries of unique elastic and plastic deformation behaviors in the NbTaTiV refractory HEA will facilitate the development of possible alloy systems for structural material applications.
